sources.title: Coupled electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cerebrospinal fluid oscillations in human sleep
sources.authors: Nina E. Fultz, Giorgio Bonmassar, Kawin Setsompop, Robert A. Stickgold, Bruce R. Rosen, Jonathan R. Polimeni, Laura D. Lewis
sources.key_finding: Simultaneous fast EEG-fMRI in sleeping humans revealed slow delta waves coupled to cortical blood-volume drops and large pulsing waves of cerebrospinal fluid surging into the fourth ventricle roughly every 20 seconds.

sources.title: The Cumulative Cost of Additional Wakefulness: Dose-Response Effects on Neurobehavioral Functions and Sleep Physiology From Chronic Sleep Restriction and Total Sleep Deprivation
sources.authors: Hans P. A. Van Dongen, Greg Maislin, Janet M. Mullington, David F. Dinges
sources.key_finding: Healthy adults restricted to 6 hours of sleep per night for 14 nights accumulated psychomotor vigilance lapses equal to 2 full nights of total sleep deprivation, yet rated themselves only mildly sleepy.

sources.title: Psychophysiological insomnia: the behavioural model and a neurocognitive perspective
sources.authors: Michael L. Perlis, Donna E. Giles, Wallace B. Mendelson, Richard R. Bootzin, James K. Wyatt
sources.key_finding: Repeatedly lying awake frustrated in bed pairs the mattress with classical Pavlovian conditioned arousal and elevated high-frequency cortical beta EEG at sleep onset, explaining why exhausted sleepers snap wide awake on the pillow.

sources.title: The human emotional brain without sleep — a prefrontal amygdala disconnect
sources.authors: 승-Schul Yoo, Ninad Gujar, Peter Hu, Ferenc A. Jolesz, Matthew P. Walker
sources.key_finding: After 35 hours without sleep, human fMRI showed a 60 percent surge in amygdala emotional reactivity paired with severed functional top-down coupling from the medial prefrontal cortex.

sources.title: Sleep Drives Metabolite Clearance from the Adult Brain
sources.authors: Lulu Xie, Hongyi Kang, Qiwu Xu, Michael J. Chen, Yonghong Liao, Meagan Thiyagarajan, John O'Donnell, Daniel J. Christensen, Charles Nicholson, Jeffrey J. Iliff, Takahiro Takano, Rashid Deane, Maiken Nedergaard
sources.key_finding: Two-photon live imaging showed cortical interstitial space expands by more than 60 percent (from ~14% to ~23%) during natural slow-wave sleep as norepinephrine drops, clearing beta-amyloid roughly twice as fast as during wakefulness.

sources.title: Sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain
sources.authors: Per Kristian Eide, Vegard Vinje, Are Hugo Pripp, Kent-Andre Mardal, Geir Ringstad
sources.key_finding: Serial multi-day human intrathecal gadobutrol contrast MRI demonstrated directly in living patients that one night of total sleep deprivation impairs tracer clearance from human cerebral cortex — and subsequent recovery sleep did not immediately erase the deficit.

sources.title: Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep
sources.authors: Natalie L. Hauglund, Mie Andersen, Celia Kjaerby, Maiken Nedergaard
sources.key_finding: Slow ~50-second locus coeruleus norepinephrine oscillations during natural NREM sleep rhythmically squeeze cerebral arteries to pump cerebrospinal fluid; sedative zolpidem suppresses norepinephrine oscillations by ~50% and cuts brain fluid inflow by ~30%.

sources.title: Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia
sources.authors: Andawei Miao, Tianyuan Luo, Boyue Hsieh, Nicholas P. Franks, William Wisden
sources.key_finding: Small-molecule parenchymal dye diffusion experiments challenged simple uniform bulk-flow models, sparking active scientific refinement distinguishing local small-dye diffusion from macroscopic slow-wave vascular perivascular pumping.

followups_replications_critiques.summary: Confirmed impaired molecular tracer clearance across living human cerebral cortex after sleep deprivation using intrathecal contrast MRI.
Identified slow ~50-second norepinephrine arterial vasomotion as the NREM pump and demonstrated zolpidem sedation suppresses that pump.
Demonstrated small injected parenchymal dyes diffuse differently than macroscopic CSF influx, sharpening the distinction between local diffusion and perivascular slow-wave vasomotion.
